SUGGESTION
(i) Shouldn’t the qualifications of the Registrar be also spelt out in the Bill?
Government’s response
 The qualifications for the Chairman and the other members of the Appellate Board have been spelt out in the Bill since
 these are statutory appointments in quasi-judicial establishment. The qualifications of the Registrar who will be
 appointed by the Central Government will be spelt out in the rules to be made under proviso to Article 309 of the
 Constitution to regulate his service. It is to be noted in this context that in the case of other Acts also like Patent Act,
 Copyright Act, Trademark Act, qualifications of the Registrar or Controller have been mentioned in the rules made
 under the Constitution. It is, therefore, proposed to follow the same approach in this case as well.
SUGGESTION
(ii) It would be preferable to clearly state in the formulation of Clause 18 that infringement means infringement done
 knowingly and willfully. The following modifications should, therefore, be done:
 In Clause 18(1) "infringed" to be replaced by "willfully infringed". In Clause 18(1) (a) "does any act" to be replaced by
 "Knowingly and willfully does any act".
 In Clause 56 and Clause 57(2) "contravenes" should be replaced by "Knowingly and willfully contravenes".
Government’s response
 We do not agree. Sub-Clause (5) of Clause 18 of the Bill is an exception to Sub-clause (1) of that Clause. The words
 "where such person does not possess any knowledge or has not reasonable ground to know" used in Sub-Clause (5)
 connote that it carves out innocent actions from Sub-Clause 91) (b) from being an infringement. The combines reading
 of Sub-clause (1) (b) and Sub-Clause (5) abundantly clarifies that only willful actions or infringement are included
 under Sub-Clause (1) (b) Such provisions are always read together at the time of interpretation. Therefore, for the
 purpose of nicety of drafting, the words "Knowledge and reasonable ground to know" have been used at only one place
 in Sub-Clause (5) of Clause (18). The same logic applied in the case of Clause 56 and Clauses 57(2).
SUGGESTION
(iii) Why should there by a difference in the retirement ages of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman which are 65 as
 compared to other members for whom it is 62?
Government’s response
 This follows the practice adopted in other similar Appellate Boards as also Tribunals. It is to be noted, in this context,
 that a member has the opportunity of becoming a Vice-Chairman after he holds office for 2 years and thus become
 eligible for the age limit of 65 years.
SUGGESTION
(iv) In Clause 38(2) "misbehaviour" should be replaced by "corruption".
Government’s response
 We do not agree. It may be noted that Article 124(4) of the Constitution has a similar expression for Supreme Court
 Judges. This expression also occurs in various Statutes of the Parliament where similar enquiry is relevant.
SUGGESTION

REPORT 71
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/71report.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:12]
(v) Why is the terms of protection 10 years?
Government’s response
 The IC designs and the ICs in which these designs are incorporated usually have a short life cycle. From the earlier life
 cycle of typically around 6 to 8 years, the life cycle has come down to 3 to 5 years due to the faster introduction of
 newer products. Article 38 of the TRIPS Agreement, however, states that the terms of protection shall not be less than
 10 years and not more than 15 years. In view of the above, it was thought reasonable to limit the term of protection to
 10 years.
SUGGESTION
(VI) How and who will decide that the design is original?
Government’s response
 As brought out in Clause 7(2), the design would be considered original if it is the result of the creator’s own intellectual
 efforts and not commonly known to the creators of layout-design and manufacturers of semiconductor integrated
 circuits at the time of its creation. The Registrar will determine originality based on the information available with him
 as also through the mechanism of advertisement of the application. If no objection is received to the claim within the
 stipulated period and the design also satisfies the other criteria in Clause 7, it would be determined as original.
SUGGESTION
(VII) Why is the period of 2 years put into Clause 7 in relation to commercial exploitation?
Government’s response
 The philosophy behind enacting the legislation to protect IPR of layout designs is to encourage the creators to register
 their intellectual property as soon as it is created without even waiting for its commercial exploitation. If a design is
 already commercially exploited, two years is considered a reasonable period for the creator to make up his mind
 whether he would like to avail of the protection offered under the legislation. If he chooses not to register his design,
 even two years of commercial exploitation, no protection would be provided.
SUGGESTION
(VIII) Clause 9 of the Bill should be deleted since it gives the powers to Registrar to withdraw acceptance of the
 application.
Government’s response
 This Clause allows for the possibility that the Registrar after accepting the application but before granting registration
 may determine it to be ineligible for registration under clause 7 and hence may decide to withdraw acceptance. In any
 case, a decision of the Registrar can be appeal-able to the Appellate Board. Hence, this Clause should not be deleted.
SUGGESTION
(IX) Doesn’t the present formulation of Clause 68(a) vest the registrar with powers in Defence matters, specifically the
 portion "which he considers prejudicial to the interest of the security of India. Should not this be "which he considers,
 in consultation with appropriate authority in the Ministry of Defence, prejudicial to the interest of the security of
 India"? Also, isn’t relates to the use of" in the explanation preferable to "requires the use of"?
Government’s response

REPORT 71
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/71report.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:12]
 This Clause was discussed at length in the Standing Committee. It was brought out that the formulation of this clause in
 the Patent (second amendment) Bill 1999 (Clause 157(a) refers) vests this authority with the Central Government and
 not with the Examiner of Patents/Controller General of Patents. The following revised formulation of clause 68, taking
 into account the concerns expressed by the Standing Committee, has now been proposed by DRDO. This formulation
 modifies 68(a) to vest the power with the Central Government, as in the case of Patents Bill, and not the Registrar.
 Also, "requires the use of" has been replaced with "relates to the use of"
SUGGESTION
(X) In addition to Clause 34(1)(a) and Clause 34(1)(b), an additional Clause 34(1) (c) should be inserted to include a
 practicing lawyer with an appropriate experience.
Government’s response
 The qualifications of the Chairman are that he is or should have been a judge of a High Court or for at least 2 years held
 the office of Vice-Chairman. These qualifications are along the lines of the Trade Marks Act. It is felt that it may be
 preferable not to expand the qualifications for appointment of the Chairman.
SUGGESTION
(XI) Is there a provision for judicial review in the Bill?
Government’s response
 As per Clause 53 of the Bill any person aggrieved by the decision or the order of the Appellate Board under this Act
 may, within the prescribed period, appeal to the High Court. As regards judicial review, provision exists under Article
 226 and Article 227 of the Constitution as also Article 136 with respect to the Supreme Court, for judicial review. Thus,
 provision exists for judicial review of administrative, quasi-judicial and judicial actions taken under the Bill and a
 separate provision for the same is, therefore, not required to be made in the Bill.
SUGGESTION
(XII) If someone is in the business of importing ICs putting them in PCBs of Computers, Television sets etc. and
 producing systems, would be guilty of infringement under Clause 18(1)(b)?
Government’s response
 Clause 18(7) of the Bill (Please also see Article 6(5) on page 18 of the background Note) clearly bring out the concept
 of Exhaustion of Rights whereby there would be no infringement of doing actions indicated under Clause 18(1) (b) if
 the IC has been put in the market by or with the consent of by the registered proprietor.
 
SUGGESTION
(XIII) The portion "or any article incorporating-------- in sub-section (5) ------- immunity from infringement" in Clause
 18(6) should be deleted.
Government’s response
 It is to be noted that Clause 18(6) is essentially an extension of Clause 18(5) which brings out the concept of direct
 innocent infringement. Clause 18(6) brings out the concept of indirect or second-hand, innocent infringement and
 establishes that the word "person" referred in Clause 18(5) includes the word "any other person" referred in Clause

REPORT 71
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/71report.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:12]
 18(6). Clause 18(5) and Clause 18(6) are, therefore, to be read together and are mutually consistent. In view of the
 above, the deletion suggested would lead to distortion. We, therefore, do not agree to the deletion.
SUGGESTION
(XIV) What is the need for Clause 24 & 25 relating to registration as registered user? Would one be required to register
 as user for getting into an agreement with a foreign company for a design which is not registered in India?
Government’s response
 The intellectual property relating IC design is a private property. The registered proprietor who is the owner of this
 property would, besides using the property himself for commercial purposes, like to license it to other users on terms
 and conditions mutually agreed to by them. Clauses 24 & 25 would ensure that the registrar would be aware of the
 authorised users and specific details of the authorisation agreed to between the registered proprietor and the registered
 user. This would also serve the purpose that may commercial use of the intellectual property without registration, as a
 registered user would imply an infringement. It is also to be noted that as per Clause 28 a registered user has the right to
 take proceedings against infringement as if he were the registered proprietor. As per Clause 29, the registered user will
 not have the right to assignment and transmission, which belongs to only the registered proprietor. It may also be noted
 that the concept of registered user is not mandated by TRIPs but is based on the functioning of the intellectual property
 rights.
 
SUGGESTION
(XV) Shouldn’t the scope of Clause 34(4) be enhanced to include the possibility of a person from the industry or
 university becoming a technical member?
Government’s response
 The philosophy behind Clause 34(3) and 34(4) is to restrict appointment as judicial member and technical member to
 persons who are part of the Indian legal Service or those having held civil judicial office for at least 10 years for a
 judicial members and a person who is holding the post of Joint Secretary to the Government of India or higher posts at
 least for 5 years with atleast 5 years experience in the area of semiconductor for a technical member. This is in line with
 the approach followed in the Trademarks Act. The idea is to have persons who have had requisite exposure with the
 Government system to legal/judicial as well as technical aspects.
SUGGESTION
(XVI) Clause 41(2) does not sound technically correct since if a part of the layout design is cancelled the remaining part
 cannot performed any useful function.
Government’s response
 It is to be noted that the portion "Provided that ------- such layout-design" of Clause 41(2) clearly stipulates that the
 remaining part of layout-design if capable of performing as an IC should be retained as registered. It follows that if the
 remaining part cannot function as IC it would not remain as registered. But the registered proprietor would still have the
 option of redesigning the IC through his own intellectual efforts and seek a fresh registration.
SUGGESTION
(XVII) Shouldn’t the word "limited" be added before "purposes" in Clause 18(2)?

REPORT 71
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/71report.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:12]
Government’s response
 It is felt that this would unnecessarily restrict the scope of scientific evaluation, analysis, research etc. and, therefore,
 should not be added.
SUGGESTION
(XVIII) In Clause 18(4) shouldn’t due credit be given to the original registered proprietor?
Government’s response
 Clause 18(4) relates to the concept of reverse engineering through scientific evaluation and research, which is permitted
 under TRIPs. This is in our favour. The design created through reverse engineering would be registered only if it
 satisfies the criteria under Clause 7. Clause 18(4) establishes that the creator of the first design, which has been used by
 another creator through the process of scientific evaluation and research to create the second original design, will not
 have any claim on the second design.
SUGGESTION
(XIX) Instead of layout, why we should not protect the mask?
Government’s response
 Protection of layout-design is in fact the protection of masks of the layout. It may be noted here that most of the
 countries including Japan, Germany, Australia etc. call this as protection of layout (topographies) while in America,
 they call it protection of masks.
SUGGESTION
(XX) Both the circuits and the layouts are the intellectual property of the creator. Which one the circuit or the layout
 should be protected?
Government’s response
 Yes, both the circuit and the layout-design are the intellectual property. In fact, to realise a circuit on silicon, a layout
 design of the circuit or mask of the circuit is required to be protected. Hence, it is necessary to protect the layout. It may
 be noted that the right confirmed by registration of a layout design shall be available to the registered proprietor of that
 layout design irrespective of the fact as to whether the layout design is incorporated in an article or not.

limit frame then it might be difficult to adhere to the time frame. The Committee pointed out to the Secretary, that today
 being a cyber age it would be pertinent to provide for the advertisement of the layout designs on electronic mode within
 seven days of filing of an application.
The Committee wanted to know whether the print-media can reproduce the application with the technical specifications
 or diagrams. It was informed that this was possible and further there were provisions for advertisements in "prescribed
 forms" which would be incorporated in the provisio to the rules, which would be framed later.
On the question of awarding compensation to the bonafide applicants against frivolous applications filed in opposition,
 the Secretary informed the Committee that this was possible and it could be brought in the powers of the Appellate
 Board while framing rules. The Committee observed that this aspect may be taken care of while framing Rules.
 In regard to the "Powers of Registrar" to decide the originality of the Layout Design, the Committee was informed that
 a Registry will be set up under the Registrar and the Registry shall comprise a set up of paraphernalia which shall
 include experts related to the technical field to decide upon the originality of the designs. The Secretary further
 informed the Committee that Clause 3(1) and 3(2) meets the requirements specifying the powers of Registrar.
A verbatim record of the proceedings was kept.
4. In view of the clarifications given by the representatives of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs etc. ,
 the Committee decided to substitute the words " as soon as may be" occurring in Clause 10(1) by the words "within
 seven days".
 The Committee adopted the Clause as amended.
5. The Committee was satisfied with the explanation given by the representatives of Ministry of Law, Justice and
 Company Affairs on the remaining points.
6. The Committee then adjourned at 4.10 p.m.

R E P O R T
 
The Department of Science & Technology (DST) has been set up to act as nodal department for organizing, co-
ordinating and promoting S&T activities in the country.  The responsibilities    of DST include, among others to formulate
 policy statements and guidelines on S&T, and also to promote new areas of scientific research and act as a Co-ordinator of
 inter-departmental S&T efforts. The department is also responsible for providing support for basic and applied research in
 universities and other institutions and high quality research in autonomous bodies, interaction in societal programmes, and
 entrepreneurship development, Science popularisation, communication and S&T Management Information System,
 promotion of commercialisation of home grown technology, support to technology development programmes, technology
 information and assessment are also part of the mandate of the department. 
2.      Besides working in the field of international Science & Technology cooperation, its activities are also oriented in the
 undermentioned fields:
(a)  Surveying & Mapping (SOI & NATMO);
            (b) Meteorology (IMD, NCMRWF); and
(c) Technology Development and Applications (TDB).
3.      In his presentation before the Committee, the Secretary, DST mentioned that in order to promote grass root level
 invention the department has set up Innovation Foundation. Swarna Jayanti Fellowships have been initiated for outstanding
 young scientists. Funds have been earmarked for improvement of S&T Infrastructure (FIST) in universities and related
 institutions. The department is also working for Kishore Vigyanik Protsahan and Technopreneur Promotion Program (TePP)
 apart from Indian Climate Research work.  The department has also established high performance computing network
 facilities for research purposes and is in the process of strengthening Seismicity Programme.  The department is trying hard to
 modernise autonomous research institutions and to set up a National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration
 (NABL).  The department also proposes to set up a Patent Facilitating Cell to provide support to scientists and technologists
 on all aspects of patenting .The department also serves as a nodal agency in the field of International S&T Co-operation.
4.      As regard the objectives and achievements of the Department, the Committee was informed that during the 9th Plan the
 Department would lay emphasis on building and sustaining a strong science & technology base in the country, developing
 centres of excellence in the frontline areas of science & technology, and modernising the infrastructure of its autonomous
 research institutions. Under the SERC scheme new initiatives would be launched to further strengthen the S&T base in the
 country in selected areas of technological importance.  The overall approach would be to promote basic research around
 outstanding scientific groups and to a large extent in the academic sector.  The SERC would be provided more autonomy and
 flexibility for better management of R&D schemes and their proper monitoring and evaluation.  Some of the important
 initiatives under the SERC include promotion of research in less endowed universities; setting up Engineering Research
 Centres in the areas of Concurrent Engineering, Bio-Engineering, Technical Acoustics etc; providing industrial research
 fellowships to work in the industry; encouraging some of the frontier areas like biodiversity, noise control, plasma chemistry,
 micro robotics, chemical engineering sciences, modern classical optics, stress biology and immunology, boundary layer
 modelling, study of atmospheric chemistry etc.  The research areas for the engineering sciences, would be in the disciplines
 like Chemical Engineering; Materials, Mining and Mineral Engineering; Robotics; Computer Engineering; etc.  Under the

72nd Report of Committee on Science & Technology
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/72ndreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:14]
 programme of Intensification of Research in High Priority Areas (IRHPA), the focus would be on setting up a few major
 sophisticated facilities and Centres in the country to pursue frontline R&D, such as electron spray mass spectrometer,
 radioactive ion beam, multi-GeV Hadron heavy ion accelerator, low energy accelerator, confocal microscopy facility etc.
5.      The National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) would be strengthened to meet the
 demands. The assessors’ training programme and the laboratory awareness programme would be intensified.  The NABL
 would be enrolled as a member of the International Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation as well as the Asia Pacific
 Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation for achieving the Mutual Recognition Agreement.
6.      National Science and Technology Manpower Information System (NSTMIS), has now proposed to set up  under the
 National Science Manpower Information System, and it is proposed to be integrated with the ongoing National Technical
 Manpower Information System of the Ministry of Human Resource Development.  An on-line access to international
 databases on S&T statistics would also be established.  In the area of technology development, a more holistic and user-
friendly approach would be adopted towards making the high technologies and products available to the society with thrust on
 technology missions, technology promotion and special technology projects through critical technology promotion, high
 technology intervention in selected export areas and promotion of NGO/society/organisation.  In respect of the Instrument
 Development Programme, it is proposed to support new projects for the development of instruments in some new areas like
 energy monitoring and management, sensors etc. besides conducting training programmes and transfer of know-how of
 instruments to industries.
7.      The new initiatives under drugs and pharmaceutical research include: drug development based on traditional systems of
 medicine like Ayurveda, Unani, and Sidha besides Homoeopathy and support to joint projects leading to drug development
 for infectious diseases.  For undertaking technology projects on a mission mode, the new areas include agro food processing,
 waterways, road transportation, electric power, telecommunication, aviation, sensors, IPR and future technology forecast for
 India for 2020.  The thrust of the S&T Entrepreneurship Development activities is on strengthening and expansion of the
 entrepreneurship development cells and the S&T Entrepreneurship Parks.  Efforts were being made to initiate rural enterprise
 development through innovative S&T based micro-enterprises in rural areas.
8.      The department under the Science communication and popularisation programme propose to impart training in S&T
 communication through short-term courses for voluntary organisations, teachers; support to popular science magazines in
 regional languages; production and screening of science films on Doordarshan; development of low-cost toys, dissemination
 of software for S&T communication/popularisation etc.  The National Resources Data Management System (NRDMS) would
 concentrate on building specialised problem oriented databases and operationalising them for real-life planning and
 administrative decision making.
9.      The Committee was informed that the activities of the State S&T Councils/Departments would be intensified so as to 
 enable them to take up major projects and its impact could be seen during the Ninth Plan.  Under the international S&T co-
operation programme, efforts would be made to strengthen bilateral and multi-lateral joint venture programmes and to expand
 and accelerate the pace of S&T co-operation with research institutions in a number of countries.  The 13 autonomous research
 institutions, being supported by the DST were to be upgraded with state-of-the-art research facilities in a phased manner.  In
 addition, funds would be provided for improvement of S&T infrastructure in universities and related institutions.
10.    The India Meteorological Department (IMD) would further intensify its high technology efforts in improving the
 accuracy of predicting severe weather, its timely warning and dissemination of its long range predictions of the monsoon. 
 The major activities proposed during the Ninth Plan include: modernisation of the observational and telecommunication
 systems, use of contemporary radar and satellite technology for better understanding of weather systems, satellite-based
 dissemination of timely warning of tropical cyclones, monitoring of seismic activities, exploitation of remote sensing data for
 agro-meteorological advisories, etc.
11.    While the Committee is happy to note that the Department  would give a thrust on consolidating the achievements made
 so far, the Committee observes that some of the areas like weather forecasting systems need a focussed attention for effecting
 improvements.  At the same time there is need to review the schemes of Swarn Jayanti Fellowships and Kishore Vaigyanik
 Protsahan and Technopreneur Promotion Programme taking into account the response received and remove the bottlenecks, if
 any, in spread of scientific temper and approach among the youth.

36.    The Committee recommends that autonomous research institutions under the administrative control of the department be
 progressively modernized.
 
DRUGS AND PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH
37.    Research for new drugs is a challenging area of research due to complexity of the biological system and disease process. 
 The scheme on Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Research was initiated in 1994-95 for promoting R&D in the drugs and
 pharmaceuticals’ sectors, development of new molecules leading to commercialisable technology towards new drug
 development, giving special thrust to the development of drugs for treatment of diseases prevalent in the Indian climatic zone
 and promoting R&D in all systems of medicines bringing together the scientific expertise existing in the country in research
 institutions and industry on a joint platform in a project mode and establishment of mechanisms and linkages so as to
 facilitate the development of new drugs by the Indian Industry and the Research Institutes.
38.    The committee was informed that the Department would continue efforts to support joint research projects for the drug
 development in the area of diseases which are of importance to our country i.e. Tuberculosis, Cancer, Gastrointestinal
 disorders like Diarrhoea, Diabetes, Hypertension, Cardio-Vascular disorders and other prevalent infectious diseases in
 particular acute respiratory infections, and food & water borne diseases etc.  Special emphasis is planned to be given towards
 development of novel drug delivery systems and "Diagnostics" for various diseases of national importance.
39.    With regard to development of " Herbal Drugs  ", the Committee was further informed that the programmes included
 standardisation of traditional medicines so far are expected to be concluded successfully. In one of the research programmes
 the active compounds in Ashwagandha, Shatavari and Amtili have been identified while in another project Proposal, a novel
 method has been standardized for the preparation of certain Asavas and Arishtas, which is more innovative and less time
 consuming.  Keeping in view the progress made in the above two projects, emphasis was also being given to development of
 " Herbal Drugs ", using traditional Indian Systems of Medicine (ISM) (Ayurvedic, Unani  & Siddha), which is widely
 practiced in India.
40.    The Committee is constrained to observe that the progress made in the field of drugs is rather slow.  It therefore
 recommends that  the Department should  speed up the pace of work in this area.  Emphasis should also be on use of our rich
 heritage of traditional system and herbal medicines.
 
SWARNA  JAYANTI  FELLOWSHIPS
41.    “Swarna Jayanti Fellowship” scheme was launched in June, 1997 on the occasion of 50 th anniversary of our
 Independence in order to support selected young scientists in the age group 30-40 to achieve world standards in basic research
 as a part of Government’s endeavour to create conditions for our scientists, technologists, academicians and industrialists to
 work in close collaboration in order to achieve integrated excellence.  In  its endeavour to strengthen basic research in frontier
 areas Government have awarded 11 Swarna Jayanthi Fellowships last year to scholars (in the age group 30-40 years) in
 different areas of science for pursuing research in their areas of specialisation.  These 11 Fellows were selected out of about
 700 applicants in the year 1998 and 6 scientists were selected in the year 1999.  The scheme covers all the requirements for
 performing at the highest level and includes in addition to an attractive fellowship of Rs.25,000/- per month to the fellows,
 provision of liberal grant for the projects including amount for purchase of equipment, research and administrative support,
 consummable, national and international travel and any other special requirement including infrastructure.
 
KISHORE VAIGYANIC PROTSAHAN YOJANA
42.    The Department of Science & Technology and CSIR have launched Kishore Vaigyanic Protsahan Yojana (KVPY) this
 year with a view to encourage Science students to take on science as a career as they advance along their education from

 secondary school level onwards up to their post-graduation.
43.    The KVPY programme is expected to move forward in 2000-2001 under the overall guidance of the National Advisory
 Committee (NAC).  It is expected that 190 new students would be selected during this year and the 100 students selected
 during 1999-2000 would also continue and Rs1.10 crores has been sanctioned for these students for the year 2000-2001 for
 fellowships, annual contingency and summer programmes.
44.    As already observed in the foregoing paragraphs, both these schemes, namely the Swarna Jayanti Fellowships as also the
 Kishore Vaigyanic Protsahan Yojana need to be reviewed taking into account the response received and remove bottlenecks,
 if any, in the spread of scientific temper and approach among the youth.
 
INDIA METEREOLOGICAL DEPARTMENT
45.    The India Meteorological Department (IMD) would further intensify its high technology efforts aimed at improving the
 accuracy of predicting severe weather, its timely warning and dissemination of its long range predictions of the monsoon. 
 The major activities proposed in this area during the Ninth Plan include: modernisation of the observational and
 telecommunication systems, use of contemporary radar and satellite technology for better understanding of weather systems,
 satellite-based dissemination of timely warning of tropical cyclones, monitoring of seismic activities, exploitation of remote
 sensing data for agro-meteorological advisories, etc.
46.    The Department sought an outlay of Rs.131.90 crores in the year 1998-99 at BE stage with a view to enhance the quality
 of forecast by upgrading some of the existing facilities for monitoring the Weather Forecasts.  The allocation was reduced to
 Rs.118.74 at the RE stage as some facilities could not materialize during the financial year 1998-99 due to non-receipt of
 some Capital Equipment, viz. Doppler Radars through DGS&D which were essential for improving the Weather Forecasting
 Systems in India. 
47.    The committee was informed that the Department of Science and Technology, under the Meteorology programme has
 significantly increased its budgetary support to Rs.144.39 crores for the year 2000-2001 from Rs.120.10 at R.E. stage and
 Rs.133.98 at B.E. stage during the last financial year. The increase in allocation is mainly intended to procure S-band Doppler
 Weather Radars, High Wind Speed Recorders, replacement of obsolete skopograph at International Airports, upgradation of
 INSAT-II E, Met Ground Segment and Earth Station, establishment of Seismo Telemetry Network for National Capital
 Region, upgradation of RTH computer etc. This state-of-the-art technology would enable IMD to provide accurate forecasts.
48.    The project “Upgradation of IMDPS system” for receiving and processing INSAT-2E will be commissioned.  Old
 AVHRR receiving equipment at New Delhi and 100 CWDS receivers installed in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu coasts
 during first phase would be replaced by improved version of equipment.
49.    50 Strong Motion Accelerographs for field stations would be procured.  Mountain Met. Centre would be established at
 Srinagar and 3 Upper Air Stations under Joint Project “Development of Mountain Met in Himalayas” in collaboration with
 Ministry of Defence would also be established in the region.
50.    Seismological Telemetry System Network for National Capital Region may be commissioned apart from Augmentation
 and operationalisation of Seismological Network and National Seismological Data Centre (NSDC) under the World Bank
 assisted Project may be taken up.
51.    The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that the target for augmentation of National Data Centre and
 Modernisation/Augmentation of Air Pollution Laboratory at Pune could not be completed by the Department and hope that
 this year the department would strive hard to complete the task taken into hands.
52.    The Committee is constrained to observe that not much attention has been paid to improve the weather forecasting
 system to ensure higher degree of precision in our weather forecasts and make the country self reliant in this field despite
 Committees observations in earlier reports.  The Committee would therefore like the Department to make concerted efforts to
 perfect the system of weather forecasting as per world class standards to ensure that our forecasts do not go awry.
SOCIETAL PROGRAMMES
53.    Under the Science and Society scheme, specific programmes for socio economic upliftment of weaker sections of the
 population in farm and non-farm sectors are proposed to be developed focussing on optimum utilization of local resources
 and skills.   Based on the success of some individual projects, co-ordinated  programmes on Animal Husbandry, Integrated
 Farming System, Fish culture in Hilly Areas, Water, Health and Sanitation are proposed to be  developed. An important
 project on extraction of vincristin/vinblastin (used in cancer treatment) from Vinca rosea leaves by women would be
 launched.
54.    A Coordinate Programme for women on cultivation, semi processing and extraction of natural dyes is being launched in
 different agroclimatic zones of the country. An intervention programme for prevention of florosis is also to be initiated in
 parts of the country, which are endemic to high concentration of fluoride in drinking water.   A programme on Rural
 Laboratory Technology would also be initiated at several places. Long term support to selected NGOs is proposed to be

 continued. Individual science and technology based intervention projects would continue to receive adequate attention in
 different sectors of economy based on people’s needs of technology and services.
55.    The Department aims at evolving and implementing specific programmes to promote applications of Science and
 Technology in order to improve the quality of life especially for the disadvantaged sections of the population.  The
 programme also aims primarily at providing technology to the weaker sections of the society so that they can derive benefit in
 terms of enhanced income, reduced drudgery. While in the previous years the emphasis was on the devlopment of appropriate
 technology packages but during the year 1999 deliberate attempts have been made to enlarge the scopoe of the activities
 thorough coordinated programmes.
56.    The Committee observes that for the purpose of societal programmes necessary inputs in respect of the size of
 population sought to be covered in a programme, its specific requirements, economic status of the population in view, past
 history including medical history, traditions and such other inputs should continue to be collected & fed into computer.  This
 would provide handy data while formulating schemes for a particular section of the society.  Such programme could be need
 based programmes.
SPECIAL COMPONENT PLAN FOR DEVELOPMENT OF SCHEDULED CASTE
57.    Under the tribal sub-plan, while, the efforts continue to encourage scientists, R&D institutions and NGOs to take up
 innovative S&T based development projects, some of the identified sectors such as animal husbandry, sustainable agriculture,
 collection, processing and producing value added products from Non Timber Forest Produce (NTFP) such as Non-edible oils
 (NEO) would be given focussed attention for development of Coordinated Programmes.
SPECIAL COMPONENT PLAN (SCP) FOR SC/ST
58.    In SCP, while on-going activities related to the programme are proposed to continue, new programmes on waste
 recycling and rehabilitation of Scavengers, Ragpickers both in urban and semi-urban area would be developed in productive
 activities connected with management of garbage including recycling of waste, conversion of kitchen waste into compost
 through vermicomposting. Other programmes such as Vegetable/Fruit Mandi Waste Management and Animal Husbandry
 also would be taken up. Action Oriented Programme aimed at improving the quality of life of the Scheduled Caste population
 in the areas of traditional skill  (both rural and urban) is also proposed during 2000-2001.
59.    The Committee notes with satisfaction that wider areas are proposed to be covered under the Plan.  Mention has been
 made about the rag pickers in the urban and semi urban areas who hail at times not necessarily from SC/ST categories. 
 Coming from vulnerable sections of the society, as they are, sometimes they are picked up for harassment by police while
 they are collecting rags in the wee hours.  Efforts should also be made to educate them about their rights and possibility of
 issuing general instructions to police and other law enforcing authorities to avoid harassment to them, should also be
 examined.  Efforts should also be made to ensure that their rehabilitation results in better standard of living.              
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY POLICY
60.    In reply to a question on the revision of the Scientific Policy Resolution of 1958, the Committee was informed that the
 Scientific Policy Resolution was still valid and did not require any major changes.  The Technology Policy Statement,
 however, requires some modifications keeping in view the changed scenario both at global and national level and the
 modifications required are under consideration.
61.    The Committee observes that the government should have a comprehensive review of the Technology Policy Statement
 with a view to decide whether to have a consolidated technological policy or different Policies- one for promotion of Science
 and the other for Technology.
SCIENCE AND ENGINEERING RESEARCH COUNCIL (SERC)
62.    The programme introduced in the year 1975 with the primary objective to promote research in new emerging and
 frontier areas of science and engineering including multidisciplinary fields and also to encourage young scientists to take up
 challenging R&D activities. The Council also helps to promote the general research capability in relevant areas of science and
 engineering taking into account the capability of the host institute.
63.    The SERC scheme is under operation for more than two decades and there have been significant contributions by
 initiating research in several advanced areas of Science & Engineering.  During the last decade has the scheme focused on
 strengthening the research infrastructure in the country particularly in the university sector in remote areas.  The new  “FIST”
 programme is likely to be operationalised during the year 2000-2001.
64.    The research projects, centres for excellence and national research facilities set up by he Department  for promoting
 research are monitored annually through group monitoring workshops and specially appointed Monitoring and Review
 Committees, for their progress and performance. These reviews are taken into account while considering continuation of the
 projects or fresh proposals from these institutions and universities. Such Review and Monitoring mechanisms exist for other
 schemes also. The activities of autonomous research institutions also come up for review and monitored by the Research
 Advisory Bodies.

65.    During the year 2000-2001 the emphasis would be on supporting more infrastructure in the university sector to tap the
 expertise available in the universities. About 300 programmes based on the inputs provided by the Programme Advisory
 Committees are likely to be approved. Some of these programmes would be in the areas of plant sciences, soft condensed
 matter physics, boundary layer modeling, crystal engineering, Earth Sciences applications for societal needs, geophysical
 exploration, Mathematical Sciences etc. About 70 SERC fellowships are likely to be supported during the year and 15-20
 SERC schools-training workshops/ brainstorming sessions may be organised in various specific areas depending on their
 needs.  
OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUNG SCIENTISTS
66.    New proposals currently under process are for setting up of State-of-the-art facilities in advanced areas. During the year
 several new facilities and groups/ centres are proposed to be set up in accordance with the objectives of the scheme.
 Preference would be given for setting up these facilities in the universities where requisite infrastructure and expertise is
 available. The on-going programmes would continue to be supported based on their review by the individual Management
 Advisory Committees.
67.    The department proposes to continue assistance to Professional Bodies programme. Necessary support would also be
 provided for printing of journals, state-of-art reports, and newsletter and for organising national and international events. At
 least 100 National/International events would be organised in selected emerging fields of science & engineering, Including
 multidisciplinary, support to at about 75 professional bodies.
68.    The SERC programme is focussed mainly in areas, which are of inter-disciplinary and inter-institutional nature.  The
 scheme is implemented under the overall supervision and guidance of SERC, an apex body consisting of eminent Scientists
 from Universities, National laboratories and Industry.
69.    The Department spent Rs.57.58 crores (Rs.56.28 Plan and Rs.1.30 crores Non-Plan) in the year 1997-98 and Rs.59.15
 (Rs.58.01 crores Plan and Rs.1.14 crores Non-Plan) in the year 1998-99.  The allocation was increased to Rs.70.54 at BE
 stage (Plan Rs.69.25 crores and Non-Plan Rs.1.29 crores) in the year 1999-2000 with further enhancement at Rs.68.94 crores
 (Plan Rs.68.25crores and Non-Plan Rs.0.69 crores) in RE of the same year. The Department has now asked for an outlay of
 Rs.69.50 crores (Rs.67.50 crores Plan and Rs.2.00 crores Non-Plan) for the said programme for the year 2000-2001.
70.    In order to continue the momentum in fundamental research the Committee observes that the Department should be
 given adequate funds by the Planning Commission/Ministry of Finance for the SERC related activities.
PATENT FACILITATING CELL
71.    In the area of patent awareness, twelve workshops are planned during the year 2000-2001. Other activities like filing of
 patent applications, monthly bulletins, quarterly updates of Ekaswa-A and Ekaswa-B databases, patent searches, responding
 to queries would continue. Some improvements may be made in Ekaswa-A and Ekaswa-B. A video film on patent awareness
 is expected to be finalised and distributed to universities, R&D institutions and other agencies. Attempts are also being made
 to develop a suitable database thorough special studies, which could be easily accessed.  It is proposed to hold some
 specialised workshops for patent attorneys, examiners, etc. on topics of current science and technology, like biotechnology
 and microelectronics.
72.    In order to provide support to scientists on all aspects of patenting, a Patent Facilitating Cell has been in operation in the
 Department. A monthly bulletin called “Intellectual Property Rights” is being brought out covering a wide range of topics like
 analysis of patent, applications filed in India, national and international news and other information relating to Patent regime.
73.    The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department for spreading Patent literacy in the country by using
 various means.  However, the Committee feels that there is much more required to be done to check the theft of vast reservoir
 of traditional knowledge available in the country.
74.    After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Science and Technology and assessing the progress of
 various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of
 Rs.779.81 crores, as sought by the Department of Science and Technology, for the year 2000-2001 under Demand No. 73,
 may be approved.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests,

2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 31st March, 2000 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of Scientific and
 Industrial Research gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various
 aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.     The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the Members and
 placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and
 Industrial Research.

R E P O R T
 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) which forms part of the Ministry of Science and Technology, provides
 financial support for industrial R&D projects and promotion of industrial research in industry.

73rd Report of Committee on Science & Technology

2.   The DSIR comprises of the activities of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), Departmental Schemes viz.
 Research and Development by Industry (RDI), Programme Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PATSER), Scheme to Enhance the
 Efficacy of Transfer of Technology (SEETOT) and National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT) and two public
 enterprises viz. National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL). 
3.   CSIR is the National R&D organisation providing scientific and industrial research for India’s economic growth and human welfare. 
 It has a country-wide network of forty laboratories and eighty field centres covering fundamental and applied R&D in all areas of science
 and technology barring atomic research, developing and nurturing S&T human resource for the country through extra mural support and
 promoting scientific talent through awards, fellowships etc. Its mission is to provide Scientific Industrial R&D that maximises the
 economic, environmental & societal benefit for the people the country.  Some of the thrust areas under the consideration of CSIR are
 catalysing civilian aircraft industry, greening of leather industry, new drug discovery through symbiosis of biodiversity, heritage of
 therapeutic knowledge and modern S&T, enhancing hydrocarbons resource base: gas hydrates, promoting National IPR movement,
 spearheading global technology leadership by industry, pioneering knowledge base exports, nurturing budding talent for science.
4.   As regards the performance and achievements of CSIR, the Committee has been informed that the impact and imprint of CSIR is
 manifested in diverse ways namely: industrial production worth more than Rs.1300 crores, productivity savings worth Rs.800 crores and
 rural employment generation of 80 lakh mandays were realised during Plan period.  Besides, 800 technology licence agreements were
 executed; 250 new technologies made available for licensing; 1140 patents filed in India and 194 abroad; 10,000 papers contributed of
 which more than 65% are in SCI journals; technical assistance rendered to about 4000 entrepreneurs, external cash-flow generated
 through sponsored/contract work of Rs.670 crores.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
5.   The financial allocation for the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research for the year 2000-2001 is Rs. 970.38 crores as
 against Rs.820.46 crores in the B.E. and Rs.823.71 crores in the R.E. of 1999-2000.
 
 
The break up of financial allocation for CSIR, DSIR and Public Sector Enterprises is as follows: -

6.   The details of budgetary projections for the programmes of the DSIR during the year 2000-2001 is given at Annexure.
7.   The allocation on the plan side has been kept at Rs.355 crores, which represents an increase of about Rs.83 crores (including
 provision of Rs.30.50 crores for North-Eastern Region & Sikkim), over the R.E. and about Rs.66 crores over the B.E. of 1999-2000.  On
 this aspect of enhanced allocation, the Committee has been informed that out of the increase of Rs.66 crores over the B.E. of 1999-2000,
 Rs.1.6 crores is for DSIR, Rs.1.4 crores for PSEs and Rs.63 crores for CSIR. 
8.   The Department proposes to undertake a new scheme namely New Millenium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) for
 which an allocation of Rs.50 crores has been sanctioned.  Its objective is to focus on a few areas which would fulfil the National
 objective of a global leadership in the technology.  The Committee has been further informed that the emphasis of this new initiative
 would be to identify four to five such areas, build a true ‘Team India’ effort inviting both the public institutions and private sector.  It has
 also been given to understand that the funds will be made available through a competitive bidding process for the individual elements of
 the programme.
9.   The Committee observes that the Department has already begun the process of putting in place a system of identifying and nurturing a
 few niche technology areas where the country could attain an undisputed global leadership position in coming decade.  However, it
 recommends that this new initiative may be accomplished by judiciously selecting technology areas where the country has a potential of
 emerging as a global leader.  While making selection of projects, it may also be ensured that these projects are directed towards the
 public good and demands of society at large, so that benefits of the scientific advances could percolate to the most deserving sections of
 the society. 
RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT BY INDUSTRY (RDI)
10.Recognising the need for developing an indigenous technological base for technology absorption and indigenous technology
 development for achieving technological self reliance, the Government has initiated several measures to encourage industry carry out
 R&D for meeting their needs and also for establishing close links between the national laboratory system and industry.  In house R&D
 units in industry provide a desirable and essential interface between
efforts within the national laboratories and the educational sector as well as production in industry.  At present there are around 1200 in
 house R&D units duly recognised by DSIR.  They employ over 50,000 R&D personnel. The R&D expenditure incurred by these units

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/73rdreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:15]
 was around Rs.2000 crores in 1998-99.  The objectives of the scheme is to bring R&D in and by Industry to sharp focus, strengthen
 linkages among in house R&D system, National Laboratory system and educational system and strengthen R&D infrastructure in
 industry and promote and support R&D initiatives of the industry.
11.The Committee  has been given to understand that the investment in R&D by the industry is about 0.8 percent of the GNP.  The
 Committee is of the view that the quantum of investments for R&D by the Industry is far from satisfactory and recommends that steps be
 taken to promote and strengthen R&D infrastructure in the industry and if necessary by giving incentives.  The Department should
 endeavour to develop  better interface with industry and strive to bring it at par with the rest of world.
SCHEME TO ENHANCE THE EFFICACY TRANSFER OF TECHNOLOGY (SEETOT)
12.An effective technology transfer process is crucial for industrial development, be it related to acquisition and management of
 technologies or export of technologies directly or indirectly.  The scheme essentially aims to facilitate acquisition and management of
 technologies, accelerate export of technologies and services, enhance the consultancy capabilities and increase awareness about the
 usefulness of consultancy services among its customers.  Development and commrecialisation of indigenous technologies is encouraged
 and international organizations concerned with technology transfer such as Asian and Pacific Centres for Transfer of Technology
 (APCTT) are supported.  The main objectives of the scheme are to provide technical and technological inputs for acquisition and
 management of technologies; accelerate technology intensive export including export of technologies, projects and service; enhance
 consultancy capabilities; and support mechanisms for technology transfer.
13.While the Committee agrees that an effective technology transfer process is crucial for industrial development, it is of the view that the
 transfer of technology being a complex and continuous process, there is a need to develop human resource to achieve desired goals.  It
 therefore recommends that the technology should be introduced to the potential user in a manner that he can understand easily and the
 successful demonstrations should be repeated for the sake of user to avoid conflicting results, which may lead to retardation in the
 process of transfer of technology.  The Committee therefore recommends the need for strong linkages between the research extension
 centres and client system.
PROGRAMME AIMED AT TECHNOLOGICAL SELF RELIANCE (PATSER)
14.Programme Aimed at Technological Self-Reliance (PATSER) covers the activities relating to technology absorption, adaptation and
 demonstration and also capital goods development.  The objectives of the Programme are to catalyse industry’s efforts in absorption and
 upgradation of imported technology and promote indigenous development of capital goods.  While DSIR support has been catalytic and
 partial, the bulk of the financial contribution in any project has been from the industry.
15.The Committee is of the view that a separate budget may be provided for the marketing of the successful  technologies and whatever
 research and technological innovations have been made they should be thrown open to potential buyers for commercial exploitation.  The
 Committee recommends that the department should focus its research activities according to the requirements of the industry.
 
16.The Committee would appreciate if it is apprised of the results of the newly launched Technopreneur Promotion Programme (TePP)
 being funded through PATSER.
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
17.CSIR today has a network of 40 Laboratories and 80 Field Stations/Extension Centres/Regional Centres located all over the country. 
 The synergy of CSIR’s competence is sought to be optimised by aligning its R&D programmes/activities more directly with socio-
economic objectives of the country focussing sharply on areas where investment can produce maximum returns.  The R&D programmes
 of National Laboratories have been broadly categorised to various socio-economic sectors.
18.While examining financial allocation for National Laboratories, the Committee observes that the planned expenditure has been
 declining whereas non-plan expenditure has been on the rise at least at B.E. and R.E. stages of last year and budgetary allocation in the
 year under review.  The Department has informed that the financial allocation of Rs.574.75 crore (which includes the NE component)
 under National Laboratories consists of Rs.182.75 crore under Plan and Rs.392.00 crore under Non-Plan.  The increase of Rs.1.75 crore
 under Plan and an increase of Rs.43.75 crore under the Non-Plan allocation is mainly due to increase in the salaries.  It has further been
 informed that as some of the plan projects, initiated in the Ninth Plan, are nearing completion (Light Transport Aircraft (LTA), Bioactive
 molecules etc.), their allocation is tapering off, thus reflecting on the near constant plan allocation for National labs.  The Non-Plan
 expenditure has been mainly increasing due to the committed liabilities on salaries and linked.  allowances to the staff arising from the
 implementation of recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission.
19.The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to fulfil its non-plan commitments with the allocations made and would not
 resort to diversion of funds from the plan to non-plan sector.  The Committee also recommends that Department should endeavour to
 raise the funds from industry by successful transfer of technologies.  The money thus earned can be ploughed back to R&D activities.
20.The Committee is constrained to find that a large amount of technology intended to benefit the villages has not found its way to the
 villages for want of publicity.  There is thus a need for wider dissemination of information preferably through mass media.
MODERNISATION OF CSIR LABORATORIES
21.An allocation of Rs.60 crores has been made for modernisation of laboratories for the year 2000-2001 as against Rs.58 crores in B.E.
 and R.E. of last year. On being asked about the status of upgradation of equipment and R&D facilities in the CSIR’s laboratories, the
 Committee was informed that modernisation of equipment and R&D facilities in CSIR is being done on the actual minimum year to year
 requirement for up-gradation and modernisation of equipment and R&D facilities and the same is proceeding as per the approved
 schedule and the desired objectives in the form of enhanced efficiency, productivity, quality have been achieved.
22.The Committee expects that the modernisation of laboratories and equipments used therein for providing various facilities should keep
 pace with the prevalent global standards and requirements of trade and industry.  The National Laboratories should be fully 
 computerised and endeavour to create better communication facilities.
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY & TECHNOLOGY  MANAGEMENT

23.CSIR has been a pioneer in spearheading stray Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) in the country.  It has set for itself a formidable goal
 of holding a valuable portfolio of at least 1000 Indian patents and 500 foreign patents by 2001.  The Department would use them for
 forging strategic alliances with some of the global technological leaders in specific areas and generate at least 1% of its R&D budget
 from IP licensing/alliances.  CSIR would also endeavour to be a national resource and an international reference Centre on IP matters. 
 Major programmes envisaged include: comprehensive protection of intellectual property generated and safeguarding against
 infringement; patent information services etc.
24.The Committee commends the efforts made by the Council in emerging as a pioneer in spreading patent literacy in the country and as
 one of the largest patent holder.  The Committee hopes that the Department could achieve the targets set for itself of achieving at least a
 valuable portfolio of 1000 Indian patents and 500 foreign patents by 2001.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Department
 should gear up to that end for pooling of traditional knowledge of excellence to check the runaway theft of country’s genetic wealth and
 ensure protection of Intellectual Property Rights for validated traditional knowledge systems such as Ayurveda.
25.Asked about the steps taken by the Department to counter the patent on Basmati rice obtained by an American company, the
 Committee has been informed that the Ministry of Agriculture is coordinating the national effort to challenge the Basmati patent and
 CSIR is assisting it by providing its know-how and IPR expertise.
26.The Committee notes with satisfaction the initiative taken in this direction.
DRUGS AND PHARMACEUTICALS
27.The Committee has been informed that the Department through its Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI) is engaged in developing
 new drugs and immunodiagnostics, technology for drugs, intermediates and products, contraceptive agents and devices and conducts
 basic biomedical studies to understand disease process and reproductive physiology and conducts systematic evaluation of natural
 resources for lead identification. Under new drug development a new molecule Centchroman has been discovered and developed by
 CDRI in the first instance as a new non-steroidal once a week female oral contraceptive, which has been introduced in the National
 Family Welfare Programme.  Also a Piperine isolated from an indigenous plant, has been developed by Regional Research Laboratory
 (Jammu) a novel bioenhancer that enables the dosages of the common anti-TB drugs, particularly Rifampicin, to be reduced by at least
 50% resulting not only in the reduction of cost of medication but more importantly in the reduced side effects such as hepatotoxicity and
 neurotoxicity.  The know how has been transferred to the industry.  Its use with other modern drugs is being pursued.  Besides, CSIR has
 developed novel and cost-effective processes for over 30 drugs as well as four drug intermediates which have been licensed and most of
 them viz; Anti-AIDS, Anti-viral, Anti-cancer, Anti-bacterials, Anti-malarial, Cardio-Vascular, Analgesics & Anti-inflammatory, Anti-
allergic, Anti-ulcer, Anti-glaucoma, Anti-inflammatory, Antihypertensive have also been commercialised.
28.The Committee recommends that Department should endeavour to develop cost effective indigenous technologies in the field of drugs
 and pharmaceuticals  keeping in view the ample biodiversity in herbal products available in our country.  At the same time effort should
 be made to develop medicines which help eliminate the sufferings and are not merely an addition to the ones already existing in the
 market.
 
FOOD PROCESSING TECHNOLOGIES AND MODIFIED ATMOSPHERE STORAGE PACKING
29.CSIR is playing a vital role in the Food Processing sector.  The R&D programmes being pursued by the Council are related to
 development of pre and post harvest technologies for a wide range of fruit with an objective to minimise wastage and increase the shelf
 life of the produce with desirable and acceptable ripening characteristics.
30.Asked whether any research was being conducted in the entire gamut of export worthy cost-effective packing to help exporters.  The
 Committee was informed that the cost-effective packaging is an integral part of technology development at Central Food Technology
 Research Institute (CFTRI), Mysore for both fresh and processed fruit and vegetables for the purpose of exports.  CFTRI has carried out
 R&D work on development of technologies based on Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP) for the extension of storage life of fresh
 fruit and vegetables and demonstrated extension of storage life of banana, mango, capsicum and tomato to 6,4,3 and 3 weeks
 respectively.  Also CFTRI, in collaboration with Agricultural and Processed Food products Export Development Authority (APEDA),
 had successfully carried out trial export shipments of mango variety Alphonso, Banganpalli and Kesar in Modified Temperature
 containers to UK.  However large scale adoption of these techniques for export of fruit and vegetables would need proper infrastructural
 facilities such as packaging houses, cold storage etc. at different centres and ports.
31.The Committee recommends that Department should take all the necessary steps for commercial exploitation of
 techniques/technologies developed in the MAP.  The Committee is also of the view that for successful demonstration and transfer of
 technology there is a need for strong linkage within and between the research extension and client system.  Moreover, emphasis should
 be given on production of farm literature in all local languages and with the help of print & electronic media so that the farmers can
 understand the message clearly.
RURAL DEVELOPMENT
32.The Committee was apprised of the various development schemes initiated by the National Laboratories of CSIR with a view to
 developing vast majority of rural masses.  It was informed that Industrial Toxicology Research Centre (ITRC), Lucknow has developed a
 low cost online water purification system that quickly makes water free from bacteria as well as removes toxic metals like iron,
 chromium, lead, zinc and nickel to safe levels.  National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), Nagpur has developed
 a sturdy, aesthetic and easily portable kit for detecting arsenic concentration as low as 0.01 mg/L, the WHO guideline limit for drinking
 water.  A superior and fast growing mint variety called Kosi that can produce three crops instead of two each year has been developed by
 Central Institute of Medicinal & Aromatic Plants (CIMAP), Lucknow.  It has also developed an environment friendly menthol based pest
 repellent to protect stored grains. Under  Technology Mission on Oil Seeds and Pulses  funded project, ten sets of appropriate low cost
 apricot seed oil extraction machines comprising, apricot decorticator, kernel sorter, meal grinder and mechanical oil extractor has been
 designed by Regional Research Laboratory, Jammu.   Regional Research Laboratory, Bhu has developed a candleless teracotta water
 filter “Terafil” made from pottery red clay, sand and saw dust mixture.  The filter brings down the turbidity of water from 100 NTU to
 0.5 to 2.0 NTU.  The know-how has been transferred to Orissa Renewable Energy Development Agency (OREDA) for propagation

 among rural masses.
33.The Committee is constrained to observe that gains of science and technology have not reached a large section of the rural masses to
 meet  their basic  needs  in respect of adequate
nutritious food at moderate cost and potable water, good health and hygiene, employment and shelter.  It therefore recommends that the

35.After making a detailed scrutiny of the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research and assessing the

 Committee is of the view that the quantum of investments for R&D by the Industry is far from satisfactory and recommends that steps be
 taken to promote and strengthen R&D infrastructure in the industry and if necessary by giving incentives.  The Department should
 endeavour to develop  better interface with industry and strive to bring it at par with the rest of world.
(Para 11)
3.   While the Committee agrees that an effective technology transfer process is crucial for industrial development, it is of the view that
 the transfer of technology being a complex and continuous process, there is a need to develop human resource to achieve desired goals. 
 It therefore recommends that the technology should be introduced to the potential user in a manner that he can understand easily and the
 successful demonstrations should be repeated for the sake of user to avoid conflicting results, which may lead to retardation in the
 process of transfer of technology.  The Committee therefore recommends the need for strong linkages between the research extension
 centres and client system.
(Para 13)
4.   The Committee is of the view that a separate budget may be provided for the marketing of the successful  technologies and whatever
 research and technological innovations have been made they should be thrown open to potential buyers for commercial exploitation.  The
 Committee recommends that the department should focus its research activities according to the requirements of the industry.
(Para 15)
5.   The Committee would appreciate if it is apprised of the results of the newly launched Technopreneur Promotion Programme (TePP)
 being funded through PATSER.
(Para 16)
6.   The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to fulfil its non-plan commitments with the allocations made and would not
 resort to diversion of funds from the plan to non-plan sector.  The Committee also recommends that Department should endeavour to
 raise the funds from industry by successful transfer of technologies.  The money thus earned can be ploughed back to R&D activities.
(Para 19)
 
7.   The Committee is constrained to find that a large amount of technology intended to benefit the villages has not found its way to the
 villages for want of publicity.  There is thus a need for wider dissemination of information preferably through mass media.
(Para 20)
8.   The Committee expects that the modernisation of laboratories and equipments used therein for providing various facilities should
 keep pace with the prevalent global standards and requirements of trade and industry.  The National Laboratories should be fully 
 computerised and endeavour to create better communication facilities.
(Para 22)
9.   The Committee commends the efforts made by the Council in emerging as a pioneer in spreading patent literacy in the country and as
 one of the largest patent holder.  The Committee hopes that the Department could achieve the targets set for itself of achieving at least
 valuable portfolio of 1000 Indian patents and 500 foreign patents by 2001.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Department
 should gear up to that end for pooling of traditional knowledge of excellence to check the runaway theft of country’s genetic wealth and
 ensure protection of Intellectual Property Rights for validated traditional knowledge systems such as Ayurveda.
(Para 24)
10.The Committee recommends that Department should endeavour to develop cost effective indigenous technologies in the field of drugs

April 18,2000
C. RAMACHANDRAIAH
Chairman,

R E P O R T
 
 
      Biotechnology is a fascinating field of science.  Mankind has used biotechnology since ancient times for wine making
 and baking.  The modern science has uncovered the scientific truth behind these processes.  It has also multiplied the
 applications of biotechnology manifold in several areas of human welfare.      Biotechnology has emerged as the
 technology, which is set to shape the future by promising food security for the world, disease resistance and control,
 sustainable environmental options and thus a more healthier world scenario and ensure optimum utilisation of the scarce
 resources such as land.  The term “Biotechnology” was first described in 1920, although the origin of biotechnology could
 be traced beyond 6000 B.C. Biotechnology involves methods employed to living systems to produce/design or modify
 certain products for selective applications.  It has since made significant advances  and has come out with products that are
 of immense use in the most important areas of health, agriculture and industry. 
2.   The challenges in the modern biology and biotechnology in the next millenium are enormous in terms of research,
 product and process development and commercial exploitation thereof.  Adequate skilled human resources are also crucial. 
 The field of biotechnology in India has already opened opportunities for commercial exploitation in high value Biologicals,
 new generation vaccines, diagnostics in human and animal health care, value addition to agricultural crops through
 nutritional improvements, pests and disease resistance. Water and salinity stress resistance are the agenda for the coming
 years towards food and nutritional security.  Solutions for environmental protection through phytoremediation,
 bioremediation and microbial technologies may be available for treatment of degraded soils, enhanced oil recovery and
 pollution remediation and monitoring.  Therefore, Biotechnology provides a tremendous scope in the form of modern tools
 and techniques for improvement of human life through poverty alleviation, upgradation of skills and self-employment to
 large sections of society  in the rural areas to provide hem sense of social security.
3.   The Committee was informed that during the year 2000-2001 a consolidated effort would be made for application of
 biotechnology for the uplift through skill development of rural population especially women and weaker sections of the
 society and that, these  initiatives would be  pursued.  The efforts made in the first three years of 9
th plan have culminated
 into transfer of about 27 applications of biotechnology, filing of 41 Indian patents and granting of 7 Indian patents and 6
 U.S. patents.
4.   The Department   envisages consolidation of many activities during the third year of the current five year plan,
 operationalisation and speedy implementation of various programmes and supporting new initiatives.  The department is
 consciously moving towards product development in addition to basic research, as is evident from  technology transfers that
 have taken place in  the previous year.  A few  more diagnostics are expected to be taken up by the industry next year.
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
5.   Based on a critical assessment of the on-going programmes and the new initiatives to be taken during the 9
th Plan, the
 Department of Biotechnology has projected an outlay of Rs.1026 crores for a

6.   The Department has sought of a plan outlay of Rs.162.97  crores against which an outlay of Rs.136.08 crores only has

 Russia and SAARC & ASEAN countries, activities related to international rice genome sequencing programme, National

7.   The Committee observes that the demand for biotech products has been steadily increasing and counting with country’s
 tremendous potential of biodiversity, scientific and technical manpower and existing infrastructure it is likely to become an
 important global player in biotechnology in the next 10 years or so.  Keeping the mandate of the Department in view the
 Committee feels that sufficient funds need to be provided to the Department so that it can carry out its  mission effectively.
AGRICULTURAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
8.   The Committee was informed that drought and salinity are two major problems  which tend to limit plant growth and
 make soils unproductive.  A novel gene p5cs (phyroline-5-carboxylate synthase) has been reported to be a functional gene
 and over expression of this gene in transgenic tobacco results in an increased production of proline. Consequently, the
 transgenic plants produced were found to be tolerant to drought and salinity. A programme to develop transgenic indica rice
 (cv.Rasi) with p5cs gene was initiated two years ago at Madurai Kamaraj University (MKU), Madurai.
9.   A protocol for high frequency plant regeneration from embyogenic calli has been confirmed by PCR analysis.  The
 transgenic plants with desired traits would be generated in coming two years and  subjected to field evaluation.
10.The concept of organic farming is capable of  ensuring good soil health, food security and  reduce  environmental 
 pollution.  The  Committee  was  informed  that  the  department  had  started
 
national network programme on integrated nutrient management for sustainable maintenance of soil health through organic
 farming.  The efforts were being made to consolidate use of various biofertilisers and biopesticide technologies in the
 farmers’ field or specific cropping system.  This would ensure optimum use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides.  The
 technologies would help in maintenance of soil health as well as ensure environmental protection.  Various programmes on
 organic farming, specially using vermi compost have also been started in farmers’ field, demonstration to SC/ST, weaker
 sections, rural and women population.
11.The Committee feels that with the rising  costs of chemical fertilisers and the accompanying  risks of degradation of soil
 fertility because of increasing resource of the fertilisers, the role of biofertilisers and biopesticides is becoming significant. 
 The Committee recommends that the Department should encourage  the use of biofertilisers and biopesticides by educating
 the farmers though print & electronic media and field demonstrations, so as to achieve higher consumption levels of the
 bioproducts and with a view to increase their yields.  
PLANT TISSUE CULTURE TECHNOLOGIES FOR LARGE SCALE PRODUCTION AND COMMERCIALISATION
12.Tissue culture is an important tool of biotechnology which can be used to improve the productivity of planting material
